meta.title: Ecru — what to wear today, from the wardrobe you have
meta.description: Every morning Ecru suggests three outfits from your own clothes for the weather, explains every score, packs your suitcase for a trip and remembers what you wore. No AI, no account. Free for iPhone.
hero.title: What to wear today — from what you already own.
hero.lede: Ecru keeps your clothes on your phone and every morning suggests three outfits for the weather and your day. Each suggestion comes with the reason why.
hero.alt: Ecru’s Today tab on an iPhone: the date, the weather with a line on what to wear, occasion chips, and an outfit card — the pieces, a score, the reason and an “I’ll wear this” button.
trust.upload.dt: Your things stay on the phone
trust.upload.dd: Photos and wardrobe are never sent anywhere.
trust.account.dd: No email, no password, no profile on a server.
trust.model.dd: Colour is arithmetic on pixels. That's the whole trick.
own.h: Lay it down. The app finds it.
own.lede: Ecru does not try to recognise your clothes. You lay a piece on anything plain that isn't its colour, and the app finds where the garment ends and measures the colour inside that edge.
own.fix.h: And when it gets the colour wrong, it says so
own.fix.p: A busy background, or a garment nearly the colour of the table, and the edge isn't there to find. Ecru doesn't quietly average the table into the answer — it says it can't see the edge, and hands you the eyedropper and the palette.
own.alt: Ecru’s colour screen: a garment on a pale bedspread, the line “Tap the item — the dropper takes the colour from that spot”, and below it the colour picked by hand with the dropper, next to the one the app worked out itself.
wedge.eyebrow: 02 · Know why the score is what it is
wedge.h: Every other app hands you a number. Ecru tells you what it is made of.
wedge.score.note: A score, and no way to find out where it came from.
quote.reason1: “Neutral, and its faint warmth matches yours — a colour like this always works”
quote.reason2: “The colour is warmer than your skin’s undertone — of the three axes, temperature is what costs the most points here”
quote.reason3: “The colour is more saturated than your natural clarity: near the face it pulls attention to itself — saturation is the biggest penalty here”
quote.reason4: “The colour is lighter than your colouring, and your face looks darker beside it — lightness is the biggest penalty here”
wedge.p: Every score is tappable, and every tap explains that particular piece: what is off about it and where it is better worn. It names the one of the three axes that cost the most points, too — temperature, saturation or lightness.
wedge.alt: A score opened up in Ecru: “How well the color suits you”, the points, the advice “Keep it away from the face” — and which of the three axes cost the most.
outfits.alt: Ecru’s Outfits tab: a “Picks · Saved · Collections” switch and, below it, outfit cards with a score — each with the reason for that score written under it.
builder.alt: Ecru’s outfit builder: a figure made of the chosen pieces, a score, and rows of candidates for top, bottom, shoes, outerwear and accessories, with the chosen ones outlined.
calendar.lede: Mark a piece — or a whole outfit — for today or any other day you forgot. Each item’s page says how many times it was worn and when last, and the calendar gives you the month at a glance.
calendar.plan.p: Plan an outfit for a day or an occasion — a birthday, an interview, a wedding. That morning it comes first on Today. Turn on notifications and the app reminds you quietly: no sound, at most once a day, and only when there’s something to say.
calendar.stats.p: Statistics show how much of your wardrobe you wore over the last three months, what has been sitting idle, and what one wear costs — if you gave a price.
calendar.alt: Planning an outfit in Ecru: a month calendar with a day selected, an “Occasion (optional)” field with suggestions — Birthday, Wedding, Interview — and a “Plan for…” button.
colortype.h: Twelve colour types — in a minute, and only when you want.
colortype.point1: The app tells you how sure it is. A confidence figure, and the runner-up type when you sit on a border. Take the quiz any time — from a photo of yourself, too.
colortype.point2: Your choice outranks it. Pick your type by hand, and add the colour you always get compliments in to your palette. The colour type never reorders your outfits.
colortype.alt: Ecru’s colour type result: the type’s name, a confidence percentage, two lines on which colours suit you, the type’s palette, and two colours to keep away from your face.
shop.eyebrow: 05 · When you’re standing in a shop
shop.h: Whether you have anything to wear it with — visible while you are still in the shop.
shop.lede: Photograph the piece, check the colour and answer three questions — and the app compares it against the wardrobe you already have. Not ready to buy? Put it on the Wishlist: the photo and the verdict are kept, and once you buy it, one tap moves it into your wardrobe.
fitcolor.alt: Ecru’s fitting-room chat: a photo of a piece on a shop rail, and under it the app showing the colour it read and asking whether that’s right.
verdict.alt: The fitting-room verdict in Ecru: “Take it. It’ll fit right in.”, how many new outfits the piece makes, the scores and the best pairs from the wardrobe, and a “To wishlist” button at the bottom.
shop.note1.h: It won't tell you what you want to hear
shop.note1.p: The verdict averages the five best pairs, not the single best one. Any garment finds one lucky match.
shop.note2.p: To hear “take it”, at least three pairs have to reach good together.
shop.note3.h: Shop light lies, and it says so
shop.note3.p: It shows you the colour it read and asks whether that's right. Say no and you set it from the palette.
quote.verdict.yes: Take it. It'll fit right in.
manifesto.eyebrow: 08 · Why there is no AI in here
manifesto.h: No model and no server — which is why every score can explain itself.
manifesto.coda: Your wardrobe, your outfits and their explanations need no network — they work in airplane mode too.
shoot.alt: Ecru’s “How to shoot” dialog: three rules — a plain background that isn’t the item’s colour, even light, the whole piece in frame — and a “Take a photo” button.
card.alt: An item page in Ecru: the photo, its facts as chips, a “Worn N times” row — when last, how often this month, cost per wear — and a small “Wearing it” button.
limits.recognise.p: Category and pattern are chosen by you, from a list.
limits.fit.h: It won't judge cut, fit or size
limits.fit.p: Colour, pattern, occasion and season. Whether it suits your shape is still your call.
faq.cost.a: Nothing. There is no subscription, no paid tier and nothing to unlock. With no accounts to keep and no wardrobes to store, there is very little to charge for.
faq.color.q: What if the photo lies about the colour?
faq.color.a: Then you tell it otherwise. Tap the item with the eyedropper, or pick the shade from the palette — and your answer sticks instead of being recalculated away. For pale neutrals the app asks first rather than guessing, because a warm bulb turns white into cream and grey into beige.
faq.move.q: Can I move my wardrobe to a new phone?
faq.move.a: Yes — as a file. In Settings, save a wardrobe backup: items with their photos, outfits, plans, the wear log, trips and the wishlist go into one archive, wherever you send it. On the new phone, restore from it. There is still no cloud and no sync — the backup is yours to make.
faq.suits.q: Why is “suits you” separate from the outfit score?
faq.suits.a: Because they answer different questions. Harmony is how pieces relate to each other; “suits you” is how a colour relates to your face. Blend them and neither can be explained.
faq.where.a: On the App Store, free, for iPhone. There is nothing to sign up for: the app asks for your language, then offers either a one-minute colour-type quiz or to start adding pieces straight away — the quiz can wait for later.
finale.lede: Ecru is for making them usable again — quietly, on one phone, with its reasoning in the open.
footer.cookies: This page sets no tracking cookies
footer.note: An independent project, not affiliated with any other company, brand, or application using the name Ecru.
privacy.meta.title: Privacy policy — Ecru
privacy.meta.description: Ecru keeps nothing that identifies you. Your wardrobe, your photos and your colour profile stay on your iPhone. This page says exactly what leaves it and what does not.
privacy.lede: Ecru is a wardrobe app that runs on your iPhone. There are no accounts and no servers holding your things. Three things do leave the phone, and this page names all three.
privacy.collect.p1: Nothing that identifies you. We do not collect, transmit, sell or share your name, your contacts, your photos, your wardrobe or your location. The app does send anonymous usage counts, with a few technical details about the device, which you can switch off — Usage statistics below says exactly what they are.
privacy.collect.p2: There is no sign-up and no login, so we have no way of knowing who you are. The usage counts carry only a random identifier created when the app is installed; it is not linked to a person or an account, and we have nothing to link it with.
privacy.device.h: What the app keeps on your device
privacy.device.p: Everything you put into Ecru stays in the app’s own storage on your iPhone:
privacy.device.li1: photos of your clothes, including the ones taken with the camera inside the app;
privacy.device.li2: your wardrobe: categories, colours, patterns and the outfits you build;
privacy.device.li3: a record of what you wore and when;
privacy.device.li4: your colour-type profile: the hair, eye and skin colours you pick — by hand or from a photo of yourself — your answers to the three questions, and the resulting type. The photo is used only while you pick colours from it; it is not saved to your wardrobe or your profile;
privacy.device.li7: your trips: the destination, the dates, the forecast for each day and the packing list with its ticks;
privacy.device.li8: your wishlist: photos and notes about things you are thinking of buying, and the app’s verdict on them;
privacy.device.li9: outfits planned for upcoming days, and the occasion you named for them;
privacy.device.after: None of this leaves your device unless you save a backup yourself (see below). We cannot see it and we cannot recover it. Deleting the app deletes all of it for good — Ecru does not sync and keeps no copy in the cloud.
privacy.permissions.li1: Camera — to photograph your clothes and, if you choose, to take a selfie to find your colour type. Photos are processed on the device. Clothing photos are saved into the app’s own storage; the selfie is not.
privacy.permissions.li2: Photo library (read) — to add clothes, or a photo of yourself for the colour type, from photos you already have. Ecru reads only the photos you pick yourself.
privacy.permissions.li3: Photo library (add) — to save a photo of an item, or a picture of an outfit, to your library when you ask it to.
privacy.permissions.li4: Location (while using the app) — only if you turn on weather, and only to look up today’s forecast. You can name a city instead and never grant it.
privacy.permissions.li5: Notifications — only if you turn them on. They are local: the phone itself schedules them, with no server and no push token, so nothing but your iPhone knows what to remind you of and when. Silent, at most one a morning; switch them off in Profile → Settings → Notifications.
privacy.permissions.after: Any of these can be revoked in iOS settings; the rest of the app keeps working.
privacy.network.p1: Ecru makes three kinds of network request, and no others. On launch it asks Expo’s update service (u.expo.dev) whether a newer version of the app’s JavaScript is available. That request carries the platform, the app’s runtime version and the update channel; as with any request over the internet, the service also sees your IP address. It carries nothing from your wardrobe: no photos, no items, no profile.
privacy.network.p2: The service is run by Expo, Inc. under its own policy: expo.dev/privacy.
privacy.network.p3: The other two are described below: anonymous usage statistics, and the weather. There is no advertising, no crash reporting and no third-party tracking SDK. The app never asks for permission to track you across other apps or websites, because it does not. When you share an outfit or save a backup, the file goes to the iOS share sheet and from there only where you send it; Ecru itself uploads nothing.
privacy.analytics.p1: Ecru counts how the app is used, through PostHog. The events are anonymous: when the app is opened and which screens are opened; when an item is added or removed, with its category only; whether the colour the app suggested had to be corrected by hand; whether the colour-type questions were finished; whether an outfit was opened, saved, worn, planned ahead or shared — for a plan, only how many days ahead and whether an occasion was named, never the name itself; how trips, the weather suggestions and the wishlist are used; whether a backup was saved or restored, with the number of items only; and whether notifications were turned on. The events themselves are numbers and short labels.
privacy.analytics.tech: Alongside each event, PostHog receives the standard technical details its library adds: that random install identifier and a session identifier, the device model, the iOS and app versions, the screen size, the language and region setting, and the time zone. Your connection’s IP address reaches PostHog as with any request over the internet; the project is set to discard it rather than store it.
privacy.analytics.p2: What is never sent: your photos or their file paths, your notes, brands or item names, the colours of your clothes, your name, your location and where you travel. PostHog is also told not to work out a country or city from your connection. No profile is created for you, and screen recording is switched off. PostHog stores the events in the European Union and acts as a processor on our behalf; its own policy is at posthog.com/privacy.
privacy.analytics.p3: Counting does not begin until you have been through the introduction and added your first item — with one exception. On the very first launch the app sends a single empty event that says only that it has been opened for the first time, so we can tell how many people leave before adding anything. It carries no properties and is sent once per install. You can switch counting off at any time in Profile → Settings → Data and privacy → Anonymous usage statistics, and that choice survives a profile reset.
privacy.weather.p1: The Today tab can show the weather and pick outfits for it. This is off until you turn it on, and the app works fully without it.
privacy.weather.p2: To look up the forecast it needs a place — either this device’s location, or a city you type in; the name you type is sent to Open-Meteo’s place search to find it. Coordinates are rounded to about 11 kilometres before they are sent, so a request says roughly which town you are in and nothing closer. Trips use the same service: to plan one, the app sends the destination’s rounded coordinates and the trip dates. If notifications about sharp weather changes are on, the app asks the same service for today’s and tomorrow’s forecast for the same rounded place when you open it. All of this goes to Open-Meteo and nowhere else, carries nothing from your wardrobe, and is not stored by us. Turning weather off erases the saved place; resetting your profile erases it together with your trips.
privacy.backup.p1: In Settings you can save a wardrobe backup as a single file (.zip): item photos, items, outfits and plans, the wear log, trips, the wishlist and your colour type. The file is put together on the phone and handed to the iOS share sheet — to wherever you send it yourself: Files, AirDrop, email or a cloud drive. We never receive it or see it.
privacy.backup.p2: The file is not encrypted, so keep it the way you would keep the photos themselves. Restoring from a backup replaces everything currently in the app; the statistics and notification settings stay as they are on this phone.
privacy.children.p: Ecru collects nothing that identifies anyone, children included.
privacy.site.p: The site counts visits through the same PostHog project (in the EU): which pages are opened, where visitors came from (the referring site or a link tag), how far down they scroll, which language they pick, and whether they tap the App Store button. There are no cookies and nothing is stored in your browser — each page load is a separate anonymous visit, and we cannot tell when you come back. No city or country is worked out from your IP, and there is no screen recording. If your browser sends “Do Not Track”, the page counts nothing at all. The link to the App Store carries a campaign tag — where you came from and which button you tapped — so App Store Connect can show which links bring people in; it says nothing about you.
privacy.rights.p: We hold nothing that identifies you. Your wardrobe is on your device and under your control: delete individual items inside the app, reset your profile (at the bottom of the Profile tab), or delete the app to remove everything at once. Backups you saved are wherever you put them, and are deleted there. The usage counts carry only a random identifier we cannot connect to you, so we cannot find yours to hand over or delete; switching statistics off in Settings stops them.
privacy.changes.p: If this policy changes, the new version appears at this same address with a new date, and anything substantive is named in the app’s release notes.
privacy.contact.p: Questions about this policy, or about the app:
today.h: Three outfits every morning — from your clothes, for the weather.
today.lede: The Today tab knows the forecast and where you’re going — sport, everyday or dressy — and picks outfits from what’s already in your wardrobe. Tap “I’ll wear this” and the day is logged.
today.picks.h: The picks grow on their own
today.picks.p: Add a piece and Ecru works it through your wardrobe straight away, topping up the suggestions. Save an outfit you like and it stays in the Outfits tab.
today.build.p: Pick the pieces yourself: the score and its reason change with every swap, and “Shuffle” offers another take when you don’t know where to start.
trips.h: The smallest suitcase for every day away.
trips.lede: Give it a city and dates — Ecru checks the forecast for each day and builds the shortest packing list that covers the whole trip.
trips.days.p: Every day gets an outfit for its own weather, and pieces repeat wherever they can — which is what keeps the suitcase light.
trips.pack.p: Tick off what’s packed and the suitcase fills up. If you’re leaving soon and it isn’t done, the app sends a quiet reminder the day before.
trips.alt: Packing in Ecru: a suitcase picture that fills with every tick, the weather for each day of the trip, and the packing list by category.
own.first.p: Forty pieces is about an hour. It speeds up from there: add several photos from your library at once and the app takes you through them one by one.
manifesto.p1: Colour is an average over pixels; the score is a formula over colour, occasion, season and pattern. That is why every suggestion can show its working instead of just saying “92%”.
manifesto.p2: No account, no cloud, no ads. Your clothes and photos stay on your phone; the only things that go over the network are the update check, the weather if you turn it on, and anonymous statistics you can switch off.
limits.device.p: There is no Android or iPad version, and no sync between devices: the wardrobe lives on one phone.
faq.offline.a: Yes. The wardrobe, outfits, explanations, planning and the fitting room all work in airplane mode. The network is only needed for the weather and a trip’s forecast.
faq.data.a: Your clothes, photos, outfits and colour type live only on your phone — we never see them. The app sends anonymous usage statistics with no photos or item names, and you can switch them off in Settings. The privacy policy has the details.
